quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Chess masters can glance at a board from a real game and reproduce nearly every piece afterward, a feat that astonishes observers. It is tempting to conclude that they possess an unusually powerful memory. Yet when the same masters are shown pieces scattered at random, their advantage largely disappears; they do no better than beginners. What they have developed is not a general capacity but a vast library of meaningful patterns, which lets them see a position as a handful of familiar groups instead of thirty separate objects. The same has been found among musicians remembering scores and programmers remembering code. Expertise, on this account, is less a matter of stronger minds than of richer knowledge in one field, which explains why it seldom carries over to others.
options: Specialized Knowledge Rather Than Superior Memory in Experts
Chess Masters Recalling Real Game Positions Accurately
Musicians and Programmers Remembering Patterns
How Practice Builds a Stronger General Memory
quests.correctAnswer: Specialized Knowledge Rather Than Superior Memory in Experts
quests.hint: The masters lose their advantage with random pieces. What does that reveal about the source of their skill?
quests.explanation: The chess result is the key evidence, and the musicians and programmers show the same pattern elsewhere. The option about practice building general memory is exactly the view the random-piece result undermines.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title states the passage's conclusion that the masters' skill lies in field-specific patterns rather than general memory power.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The two-day weekend feels like a natural feature of the calendar, but it is barely a century old in most countries. For most of history, work followed the demands of seasons, crops, and religious observance rather than any fixed rhythm of rest. Factories introduced regular hours, and workers gradually won a half day off, then a full one, largely through organized negotiation rather than employers' generosity. When some factories found that rested workers produced more, the second day became easier to defend. Even now, the arrangement varies: some countries rest on Friday and Saturday, others on Saturday and Sunday. What appears to be a law of nature is a settlement, reached through argument, and open to revision whenever people decide that a different balance would serve them better.
options: Different Days of Rest in Different Countries
Shortening of the Modern Working Week
Factories Finding That Rested Workers Produce More
The Negotiated Settlement Behind the Weekend
quests.correctAnswer: The Negotiated Settlement Behind the Weekend
quests.hint: The last sentence contrasts a 'law of nature' with something else. What is the 'something else'?
quests.explanation: Factory productivity and country differences are evidence in the account, and the shortening of the working week is never traced. The thesis is that the weekend was negotiated and can change.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice captures the last sentence's claim that the weekend is a negotiated arrangement rather than a natural rule.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Few people admire the standard screw thread, yet modern manufacturing depends on it. Before such standards, each maker cut screws to a private design, so a lost nut could not be replaced with a purchased one, and repairs required returning to the original workshop. Once threads were standardized, parts became interchangeable, shops could specialize, and engineers could design machines around components they knew would exist. Standards seem to restrict freedom by limiting choice, but the effect has been the reverse: agreeing on the dull details freed effort for the interesting ones. The same logic applies to electrical plugs, shipping containers, and file formats, where boring agreements are the foundation on which visible innovation is built.
options: The Limits That Standards Place on Choice
Dull Standards Enable Innovation
Interchangeable Screws and Replaceable Nuts
Everyday Objects Governed by Technical Standards
quests.correctAnswer: Dull Standards Enable Innovation
quests.hint: Ask what the passage says standards do for creative work, despite seeming to limit it.
quests.explanation: Interchangeable screws are the central example, and the limits on choice are the objection the passage answers. A list of regulated objects only repeats the examples without reaching the paradox.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title states the paradox the passage develops: agreement on dull details enables innovation.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The word 'natural' appears on everything from snacks to shampoo, and shoppers often treat it as a promise of safety. Yet the word has no fixed legal meaning in many places, and the natural world contains poisons, allergens, and pathogens that no manufacturer would knowingly add. A plant extract may irritate skin more than a synthetic compound designed to be gentle; a preservative made in a laboratory may protect food that would otherwise spoil dangerously. None of this means that synthetic is better. The point is that origin is a poor guide to effect. Assessing a product by what it contains and how it behaves is harder than trusting a label, but it is the only approach that fits the evidence.
options: Labels That Have No Fixed Legal Meaning
Why Laboratory Ingredients Deserve More Trust
Judging Products by Effect, Not by the Word 'Natural'
Plant Extracts That Irritate Sensitive Skin
quests.correctAnswer: Judging Products by Effect, Not by the Word 'Natural'
quests.hint: The passage says 'None of this means that synthetic is better.' What does it say instead?
quests.explanation: Plant extracts and legal meaning are supporting points. The option favoring laboratory ingredients is the very claim the passage says does not follow from its argument.
quests.whyThisTitle: It expresses the passage's conclusion that a product should be judged by what it does, not where it comes from.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When analysts showed that a three-point shot is worth more, on average, than a long two-point shot, basketball teams took notice. Within a decade, shot patterns changed across the sport: fewer mid-range attempts, more from beyond the arc and near the basket. The gain in scoring efficiency was real. Yet some coaches and fans complain that games have become repetitive, since every team now follows the same logic. A statistic that improves performance can also narrow the range of styles and reduce the variety that made the sport interesting. The episode illustrates how measurement, once it is trusted, does more than describe a game; it starts to steer it.
options: Analytics Reshaping the Game
Three-Point Shots Outscoring Long Two-Pointers
Games Becoming Repetitive for Spectators
How Data Made Basketball More Efficient
quests.correctAnswer: Analytics Reshaping the Game
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence uses 'more than describe.' What does measurement do beyond describing?
quests.explanation: The shot values and repetitive games are evidence. The efficiency option covers only the gain in scoring and leaves out the passage's real point: trusted measurement began to steer the game.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the passage's point that the numbers began to shape how the game is played.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When most students receive top grades, the grades lose their power to distinguish one student from another. Employers and graduate schools respond by relying on other signals: the reputation of the institution, letters of reference, entrance tests. Ironically, this can disadvantage the very students that generous grading is meant to help, since they are less likely to have well-connected referees. Teachers who inflate grades usually do so with kind intentions, seeking to spare pupils discouragement and to avoid disputes. The consequence, however, is that a mark stops carrying information, and information is what makes a mark worth giving. A grade that cannot tell anything is a courtesy, not an assessment.
options: Kind Intentions Behind Generous Marking
Why Top Grades Stop Telling Us Anything
Employers Relying on Letters of Reference
How Teachers' Kindness Undermines Fair Assessment
quests.correctAnswer: Why Top Grades Stop Telling Us Anything
quests.hint: Which sentence gives the reason why generous grades lose their value?
quests.explanation: Letters of reference and kind intentions belong to the account. Teachers' kindness is a cause the passage mentions, while its main point is that grades without variation carry no information.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title states the central claim that grades lose meaning when nearly everyone receives the top mark.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A vaccine that works perfectly in the laboratory may fail to protect anyone if it spoils on the way to a remote clinic. Many vaccines must be kept within a narrow temperature range from factory to arm, a requirement known as the cold chain. In regions with unreliable electricity, keeping refrigerators running can be as challenging as developing the vaccine itself. Public health programs have therefore invested in solar-powered fridges, insulated carriers, and temperature monitors that alert workers when a shipment has warmed. The lesson is not confined to medicine: an invention delivers benefit only when it can be brought reliably to those who need it, and the logistics of delivery deserve the same attention as the science of discovery.
options: Why Delivery Matters as Much as Discovery
Cold Chain in Global Health Programs
Solar-Powered Fridges for Remote Clinics
Temperature Limits on Vaccine Storage and Transport
quests.correctAnswer: Why Delivery Matters as Much as Discovery
quests.hint: Look at how the final sentence says the lesson is 'not confined to medicine.' What general lesson is it?
quests.explanation: Solar fridges and temperature limits are details of the cold chain, which is only the medical example. The final sentence says the lesson is not confined to medicine: delivery matters as much as discovery.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice expresses the general lesson the vaccine example illustrates.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Poets have written sonnets for centuries under strict rules of length and rhyme, and cartoonists must fit a joke into three small frames. It might seem that such limits would stifle imagination. Many artists report the opposite: a blank page with unlimited possibilities can be paralyzing, whereas a constraint gives a starting point and turns the task into a puzzle. The struggle to fit an idea into a small space forces choices, and choices produce originality. This does not mean that every restriction helps; rules that are arbitrary or excessive can crush creativity. But well-chosen limits appear to direct effort rather than block it, which is why teachers of writing so often begin with a set of restrictions instead of a free topic.
options: Why Free Choice Produces the Best Art
Cartoonists Fitting Jokes into Three Small Frames
Paralysis of a Blank Page
How Constraints Spur Creative Work
quests.correctAnswer: How Constraints Spur Creative Work
quests.hint: The passage includes a qualification. Which title keeps the claim and the qualification?
quests.explanation: Cartoonists and the blank page are supporting points. The option praising free choice is the belief the passage argues against, since it says appropriate limits direct creative effort.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title captures the claim that well-chosen limits direct creative effort.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In negotiations, the party that seems to be in a hurry is usually at a disadvantage. A buyer who must close a deal by Friday, or a seller who needs cash this month, will accept terms that a more patient counterpart would refuse. Skilled negotiators therefore work to protect their alternatives and to hide their deadlines. This is not a matter of pretense alone; those with genuine alternatives, such as another buyer or another job offer, can afford to wait because waiting costs them little. Patience, then, is less a personality trait than a product of circumstances that can be prepared in advance. The best time to build bargaining power is long before the meeting begins.
options: Bargaining Strength Built Before the Meeting
The Psychology of Deadlines in Business Deals
Buyers Forced to Close by Friday
Hiding Deadlines, Protecting Alternatives
quests.correctAnswer: Bargaining Strength Built Before the Meeting
quests.hint: The passage says patience is 'less a personality trait than a product of circumstances.' What follows?
quests.explanation: Hidden deadlines and rushed buyers are parts of the discussion, and the psychology of deadlines is touched on but is not the point. The message is that leverage comes from alternatives prepared in advance.
quests.whyThisTitle: It states the closing claim that bargaining power is built ahead of time through real alternatives.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Governments often describe benefits by their value, but citizens experience them through forms, queues, and repeated proofs of identity. Researchers call these frictions the 'time tax': hours spent proving eligibility for help that the state has already decided to give. The burden falls unevenly. People with stable jobs, internet access, and confident language skills manage it easily, while those in greatest need often give up. When programs simplify applications, such as by filling in known information automatically, more eligible people receive support, without any change in the rules of eligibility. This suggests that some of what looks like a shortage of generosity is, in fact, a shortage of good design.
options: Stable Workers Managing Forms Easily
Unequal Access to Government Services by Income
The Hidden Barrier of Paperwork in Public Help
Filling In Known Information Automatically
quests.correctAnswer: The Hidden Barrier of Paperwork in Public Help
quests.hint: The last sentence contrasts two possible explanations. Which does the passage favor?
quests.explanation: Automatic form-filling and stable workers are elements of the argument, and unequal access is one observation within it. The main claim is that complicated procedures keep eligible people from receiving help.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the claim that poor procedure design, not stingy rules, keeps help from those who need it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Supporters of a losing team often attract puzzled sympathy: why devote weekends and money to something that repeatedly disappoints? The question assumes that fans want victory above all. Studies of supporters suggest a different picture. Fans describe the club as a shared inheritance, passed from parents, and the stadium as a place where strangers become a community. Winning is welcome, but the identity does not depend on it; in some ways, enduring a poor season together strengthens the bond. A supporter who abandoned the team at the first losses would, in the eyes of others, have missed the point. Loyalty of this kind is less a wager on results than a way of belonging.
options: How Sports Clubs Pass Between Generations
Stadiums Turning Strangers into a Community
Sympathy for Supporters of Losing Teams
Belonging Rather Than Winning Behind Fan Loyalty
quests.correctAnswer: Belonging Rather Than Winning Behind Fan Loyalty
quests.hint: The opening question rests on an assumption. What does the passage say is wrong with it?
quests.explanation: The stadium community is one piece of evidence, and the sympathy is where the passage begins. Passing a club between generations is one description of belonging, not the answer to the opening question.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title states the passage's answer to its opening question: fans are bound by belonging rather than results.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When people are insured against a loss, they sometimes take less care to avoid it: a driver with full coverage may park less carefully, a company protected by guarantees may take bigger risks. Economists call this moral hazard, and it is often cited as a reason to be wary of protection. Yet the argument can be pushed too far. Insurance also allows people to attempt ventures they would otherwise avoid, such as starting a business or lending money, and many losses are beyond anyone's control. Insurers therefore design policies that keep some risk with the insured, through deductibles or co-payments. The aim is not to eliminate the behavior but to balance protection against the temptation to be careless.
options: How Insurance Balances Protection and Risk
How Insurance Encourages Risky Behavior
Deductibles and Co-Payments in Insurance Policies
Drivers Parking Less Carefully with Full Coverage
quests.correctAnswer: How Insurance Balances Protection and Risk
quests.hint: The passage says the argument 'can be pushed too far.' What does it recommend in its place?
quests.explanation: Deductibles and careless parking are elements of the picture. Encouraging risky behavior is only the problem the passage acknowledges before explaining how insurers balance it.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice reflects the last sentence's aim of balancing protection with the risk of carelessness.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The vivid colors in photographs of distant galaxies and microscopic cells are not what a person would see through the instrument. Many of these images are assembled from measurements of light that human eyes cannot detect, and colors are assigned to represent different wavelengths or chemical properties. Some viewers feel deceived on learning this. Scientists reply that the colors are choices made to communicate real differences in the data, in the way a map uses blue for water without pretending that the sea is painted. The images are not simply records; they are interpretations, designed to make invisible structure visible. A viewer who understands this can enjoy them with informed appreciation instead of naive trust.
options: Viewers Feeling Deceived by Bright Colors
Colors Assigned to Different Wavelengths
How Colors Are Chosen for Astronomy Photographs
The Interpretation Built into False-Color Images
quests.correctAnswer: The Interpretation Built into False-Color Images
quests.hint: The passage compares the images to a map. What does that comparison suggest about them?
quests.explanation: Assigned colors and viewers' feelings are parts of the account. Astronomy photographs alone is too narrow, since the passage also includes microscopic cells and makes a general point about interpretation.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title captures the idea that the colors are deliberate choices that communicate real differences.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: An experienced baker can tell by touch when dough is ready, and a veteran mechanic can diagnose an engine by its sound. Asked to explain, they often struggle; the knowledge lives in their hands and ears rather than in words. Researchers call it tacit knowledge, and it explains why manuals, however detailed, cannot replace apprenticeship. Learners absorb it by working beside someone skilled, imitating and being corrected, over months or years. Organizations that lose experienced staff without arranging such transfer often discover that something important has vanished, though it appeared nowhere in their records. What can be written down is only part of what people know.
options: Bakers Judging Dough by Touch
How Apprenticeship Trains Skilled Workers
Tacit Knowledge and the Limits of Written Instructions
Organizations Losing Experienced Staff
quests.correctAnswer: Tacit Knowledge and the Limits of Written Instructions
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence gives a limit. What is it a limit on?
quests.explanation: Bakers and lost staff are an example and a consequence. Apprenticeship is the remedy the passage mentions, not the concept it develops, which is that some knowledge cannot be written down.
quests.whyThisTitle: It states the concept the examples illustrate and the limit it places on written instruction.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Trust in an institution is slow to build and quick to lose, and after a scandal, the usual response is an apology followed by a promise to reform. Research on organizations that recovered suggests that words matter less than costly action: opening records to outside review, accepting consequences for those responsible, and changing the incentives that allowed the failure. Such measures are uncomfortable precisely because they reduce the organization's control. That discomfort is what makes them credible. A change that costs nothing invites suspicion that nothing has changed. Rebuilding trust, in short, requires visible sacrifice, not merely visible regret.
options: The Path Back to Trust Through Costly Action
Opening Records to Outside Review
Trust Taking Long to Build and Little Time to Lose
How Institutions Apologize After a Scandal
quests.correctAnswer: The Path Back to Trust Through Costly Action
quests.hint: Look at how the last sentence contrasts 'sacrifice' with 'regret.' What is the passage saying?
quests.explanation: Outside review is one costly action, and slow trust-building is the opening premise. The apology is only where the discussion begins; the passage argues that apologies alone are not enough.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title states the conclusion that credibility comes from changes that cost the organization something.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Asked to name the greatest medical advances, many people mention antibiotics or vaccines. Historians of public health often add something less dramatic: clean water and sewage systems. Cities that built them in the nineteenth century saw death rates from waterborne disease fall dramatically, long before effective treatments existed. The improvement came not from curing individuals but from stopping infection at the source. Such measures are easy to overlook because their success is invisible: nothing happens, and no patient is saved in a dramatic moment. Yet prevention at scale has saved more lives than most treatments, which is why its neglect is a recurring mistake in public policy.
options: Sewage Systems Built in Nineteenth-Century Cities
The Greatest Advances in Modern Medicine
Invisible Successes That People Overlook
The Under-Appreciated Power of Sanitation and Prevention
quests.correctAnswer: The Under-Appreciated Power of Sanitation and Prevention
quests.hint: What does the passage say about why prevention gets overlooked, and why that matters?
quests.explanation: Sewage systems and invisible successes are parts of the argument. Medical advances in general is broader than the passage's focus on quiet prevention and its neglect.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title covers the neglected measures, their achievements, and the mistake of undervaluing them.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Writing a to-do list does more than remind people of tasks; it frees the mind from the effort of keeping them in view. Psychologists have found that unfinished tasks tend to nag at attention, and that making a specific plan for when and where to complete them reduces the intrusion, even before anything is done. The mind, it seems, is satisfied by a trustworthy external record. This has led some researchers to see notebooks, calendars, and reminders not as crutches but as extensions of memory that let us think about other things. The practical implication is that people who feel overwhelmed may benefit less from trying to remember more than from deciding what to hand over to a reliable system.
options: Trusted Lists That Extend Memory
Improving Memory to Handle a Busy Life
Making a Plan for When to Do Tasks
Unfinished Tasks Nagging at Attention
quests.correctAnswer: Trusted Lists That Extend Memory
quests.hint: The passage rejects one way of describing notebooks and calendars. What does it put in its place?
quests.explanation: Planning and nagging tasks are evidence. Improving memory is the opposite of the passage's advice, which is to hand tasks to a reliable external system.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice states the view that reliable records extend memory and relieve attention.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Two methods dominate advice on paying off several debts. The 'avalanche' targets the highest interest rate first, which minimizes total cost. The 'snowball' targets the smallest balance first, which clears whole accounts quickly and provides a sense of progress. On paper, the avalanche wins. In practice, studies of borrowers suggest that those who use the snowball are more likely to stay with their plan, because visible early victories sustain motivation. The best method, therefore, is not the one with the best arithmetic but the one a person will actually follow through to the end. Financial planning succeeds or fails on behavior at least as much as on calculation.
options: Why the Avalanche Method Saves the Most Money Overall
Targeting the Highest Interest Rate First
Motivation Versus Arithmetic in Paying Off Debt
Clearing Small Balances for Quick Progress
quests.correctAnswer: Motivation Versus Arithmetic in Paying Off Debt
quests.hint: The passage says 'On paper, the avalanche wins.' What does it say in practice?
quests.explanation: The avalanche and the snowball are the two methods compared. The avalanche's savings are true on paper but are not the passage's point, which is that follow-through can outweigh mathematical efficiency.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the tension between the mathematically best plan and the one people will stick to.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Concertgoers and critics often praise the acoustics of famous old halls, and a great many musicians agree. In blind tests, however, listeners have had difficulty distinguishing recordings made in celebrated venues from those made in ordinary ones, and audiences' ratings seem to be influenced by what they were told beforehand. This does not prove that all halls sound the same; measurements do show real differences in echo and clarity. What it shows is that perception is shaped by expectation, so that a hall with a reputation begins with an advantage. Acousticians therefore try to test sound with instruments and with listeners who do not know which room they are hearing.
options: Blind Tests Comparing Recorded Sound
How Reputation Shapes What We Hear in Halls
Why Famous Halls Sound Better Than Ordinary Ones
Real Differences in Echo and Clarity
quests.correctAnswer: How Reputation Shapes What We Hear in Halls
quests.hint: The passage says 'This does not prove that all halls sound the same.' What does it prove?
quests.explanation: Blind tests and measured differences are evidence. The belief that famous halls simply sound better is what the blind tests call into question; the conclusion is that expectation influences what listeners hear.
quests.whyThisTitle: It states the finding that listening is shaped by expectation as well as by the room.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The shift to electric vehicles and renewable power depends on minerals such as lithium, cobalt, and copper, and demand for them is rising quickly. Extracting them carries costs: mining can consume water, damage ecosystems, and, in some places, take place under poor labor conditions. These facts are sometimes used to argue that the transition is not worth pursuing, but the comparison is incomplete, since fossil fuels also require continuous extraction and produce emissions. The more accurate conclusion is that every energy path carries costs, and that the useful question is which costs are smaller, better managed, and easier to reduce, for example through recycling and more careful sourcing.
options: Mining Damage to Water and Ecosystems
Weighing Mineral Mining Against the Costs of Fossil Fuels
Why Green Technology Depends on Mining
Recycling to Reduce the Need for New Mining
quests.correctAnswer: Weighing Mineral Mining Against the Costs of Fossil Fuels
quests.hint: The passage calls one comparison 'incomplete.' What does it say the complete comparison is?
quests.explanation: Recycling and mining damage are pieces of the discussion. Dependence on mining is only one side of a comparison the passage says must include the costs of fossil fuels.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the balanced comparison the passage recommends between mining and fossil fuels.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A large study found that a new teaching method raised test scores by a statistically significant margin, and the result was widely reported. Closer reading showed that the average gain was less than one point on a hundred-point scale. With enough participants, even tiny differences become statistically detectable, meaning that they are unlikely to be due to chance. But whether a difference matters in practice is a separate question that no calculation of probability can answer. Readers of research should therefore ask two questions: is the effect likely to be real, and is it big enough to care about? A finding can pass the first and fail the second.
options: How Statistical Tests Measure Chance
A One-Point Gain on a Hundred-Point Scale
Statistical Significance Versus Practical Importance
Large Studies Detecting Tiny Differences
quests.correctAnswer: Statistical Significance Versus Practical Importance
quests.hint: The last sentence says a finding can pass one test and fail another. What are the two tests?
quests.explanation: The one-point gain and the large-study effect are parts of the explanation. How tests measure chance covers only the first half of the passage's distinction between a real effect and an important one.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title names the distinction between a real effect and a meaningful one that the passage develops.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many products now resist repair: screws are replaced by glue, parts are sold only to authorized centers, and software checks whether a replaced component is 'genuine'. Manufacturers argue that the limits protect safety and quality. Repair advocates respond that they also protect sales, since a repairable product is one that people replace less often. Studies of consumer behavior suggest that when repair is easy and cheap, products stay in service longer, reducing waste and spending. The dispute raises a question about ownership: whether buying an object includes the right to maintain it, or only the right to use it until it fails.
options: Products Staying in Service Much Longer After Repair
The Question of Ownership Behind the Repair Dispute
Software That Checks for Genuine Parts
How Manufacturers Defend Limits on Repair
quests.correctAnswer: The Question of Ownership Behind the Repair Dispute
quests.hint: The last sentence steps back from the two arguments to ask something bigger. What is it asking?
quests.explanation: Genuine-parts checks and longer product life are details of the dispute. The manufacturers' defense is one side, whereas the passage ends by framing the whole conflict as a question about ownership.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice captures the way the passage turns a product dispute into a question about the rights of owners.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A monument is built to fix a memory in place, but the meanings it carries shift as people change. A statue raised in celebration may, a century later, be a source of pain for some and pride for others, and communities disagree over what should be done. Options range from removal to relocation to adding new plaques that give a fuller account. Historians point out that monuments tell us as much about the era that raised them as about the events they commemorate, so that even a contested monument is a useful record of a past attitude. How a society treats its memorials is, in this sense, a statement about how it treats its own history.
options: Adding Plaques That Give a Fuller Historical Account
Changing Attitudes Recorded in Monuments
Communities Disagreeing About a Statue
Why Communities Choose to Remove Statues
quests.correctAnswer: Changing Attitudes Recorded in Monuments
quests.hint: The historians make a point about what monuments reveal. What is it?
quests.explanation: The plaques and the disagreement are parts of the situation. Removal is one of several options the passage lists, and the historians' point is that monuments record the attitudes of their time.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the historians' view that monuments document both past attitudes and changing views.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Having paid for a ticket, many people attend a concert they no longer want to see, reasoning that the money would otherwise be wasted. Yet the money is gone whether they attend or not; the only real question is whether the evening is worth more than the alternatives. Economists call the error the sunk-cost fallacy, and it appears at every scale, from finishing a poor meal to continuing a failing project because of the years already invested. The remedy is straightforward in principle: ignore what has been spent and decide on what is still to come. In practice, it feels like admitting a mistake, which is why it is so hard.
options: Attending a Concert You No Longer Want
Why Money Already Spent Cannot Be Recovered
The Sunk-Cost Trap and How to Avoid It
The Discomfort of Admitting a Mistake
quests.correctAnswer: The Sunk-Cost Trap and How to Avoid It
quests.hint: The concert is an example. What general error does it illustrate, and what is the remedy?
quests.explanation: The concert and the discomfort are parts of the discussion. The lost money is a premise of the argument, not its conclusion, which explains the error and how to avoid it.
quests.whyThisTitle: It names the error and reflects the remedy the passage recommends.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: There is more to read, watch, and listen to than anyone could finish in a thousand lifetimes, and the sense of falling behind is common. Some people respond by trying to consume as much as possible, using summaries and faster playback. Others choose a smaller circle of sources they trust and accept that most things will pass them by. The second approach can look like a loss, but it protects the time needed to think about what has been read. Curating is therefore less a limit on knowledge than a condition of it: understanding depends on what is taken in slowly enough to be digested, not on the quantity encountered.
options: Using Summaries and Faster Playback
The Feeling of Falling Behind
Selective Reading and Understanding
Coping with More Content Than Anyone Can Finish
quests.correctAnswer: Selective Reading and Understanding
quests.hint: The passage says curating is 'less a limit on knowledge than a condition of it.' What does it mean?
quests.explanation: Summaries and falling behind are parts of the first approach. Coping with too much content is the problem the passage starts from, not its stance that choosing fewer sources supports deeper understanding.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title states the claim that selectivity makes real understanding possible.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In 1854, a physician in London plotted deaths from cholera on a map of a single district and noticed that they clustered around one water pump. Authorities, who had blamed bad air, were skeptical, but when the pump's handle was removed, the outbreak declined. The map did not prove the mechanism, and later evidence was needed to establish that contaminated water carried the disease. Its value was different: it turned scattered cases into a visible pattern, and made an explanation testable. Visual displays of data continue to serve this purpose; they do not replace analysis, but they show where analysis should look.
options: Origins of Modern Disease Mapping
Visual Data That Guides Analysts
Authorities Blaming Bad Air for Cholera
A Pump Handle Removed During an Outbreak
quests.correctAnswer: Visual Data That Guides Analysts
quests.hint: The passage says the map 'did not prove the mechanism.' What was its value instead?
quests.explanation: The pump handle and the authorities' view are events in the story. The origins of disease mapping is a broader history, whereas the last sentence says visual displays show where analysis should look.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title reflects the value the passage assigns to the map: revealing a pattern that guides analysis.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Studies of expert predictions have found that famous commentators are often little better than chance at forecasting events, and that confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. Those who do better tend to share a style: they draw on many sources rather than one grand theory, they update forecasts as evidence arrives, and they think in probabilities instead of certainties. Such forecasters are less entertaining on television, where bold claims attract attention. The finding suggests that the qualities that make a good performer and a good predictor can pull in different directions, and that anyone using forecasts should notice which of the two they are listening to.
options: Updating Predictions as Evidence Arrives
Traits of Accurate Versus Famous Forecasters
Bold Claims Attracting Attention on Television
Why Expert Forecasts Are Often Little Better Than Chance
quests.correctAnswer: Traits of Accurate Versus Famous Forecasters
quests.hint: Look at how the last sentence contrasts a good performer with a good predictor. What is the lesson?
quests.explanation: Updating predictions and bold claims are points within the comparison. Forecasts being little better than chance covers only the first half; the passage separates accurate forecasters from prominent ones.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice captures the contrast between traits that earn attention and traits that produce accuracy.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Analogies are the scientist's best tool for explaining unfamiliar ideas: the atom as a small solar system, electric current as flowing water. They give listeners something familiar to hold. But every analogy also misleads, because the resemblance is only partial. Students who picture electrons orbiting like planets may struggle when they meet quantum descriptions in which that picture fails. Good teachers therefore name the limits of an analogy along with its uses, and replace it with a more accurate one as understanding grows. Analogies work best when treated as scaffolding, useful for climbing and meant to be taken down.
options: Electric Current as Flowing Water
Picturing Electrons Orbiting Like Planets
How Analogies Mislead Students of Science
Analogies That Work Like Temporary Scaffolding
quests.correctAnswer: Analogies That Work Like Temporary Scaffolding
quests.hint: The final sentence gives an image of its own. What does it say about how analogies should be used?
quests.explanation: The electron picture and the water analogy are examples. Analogies misleading students is only half the point, since the passage advises using them as temporary supports and replacing them.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title expresses the closing image of analogies as supports that are eventually removed.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Debates about what schools should teach often assume that the aim is to transfer information, and each new demand, from finance to coding, is added to an already crowded timetable. Critics argue that facts age quickly and that graduates need something more durable: the ability to learn, to evaluate claims, and to work with others. Defenders of traditional content reply that thinking skills cannot be exercised in a vacuum; one must think about something, and knowledge supplies the material. Both points have force, which suggests that the choice between content and skills is a false one. Skills develop through content, and content is retained when it is used.
options: Content and Skills as Partners, Not Rivals
Adding Finance and Coding to Timetables
Facts Becoming Outdated Faster Than Curricula
Why Durable Skills Matter More Than Facts
quests.correctAnswer: Content and Skills as Partners, Not Rivals
quests.hint: The passage presents two camps and then a conclusion. What does the conclusion say about the choice?
quests.explanation: Crowded timetables and outdated facts are aspects of the debate. Durable skills over facts is one camp's view, while the passage concludes that content and skills develop each other.
quests.whyThisTitle: It states the conclusion that content and skills develop together.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Large organizations have resources, but small ones often innovate faster. A small workshop can try an idea on Monday and abandon it on Friday, while a large firm must consult several departments before a trial is approved. Yet size brings advantages that smaller groups lack: the ability to test ideas at scale, absorb failures, and reach many customers. The pattern that emerges in many industries is a division of labor. Small groups explore risky ideas, and large ones adopt those that prove themselves. Neither type can easily do the other's job, which is why healthy sectors usually contain both.
options: Large Firms Consulting Several Departments
Trying and Abandoning Ideas Within a Week
Why Small Organizations Innovate Faster
Why Sectors Need Small and Large Firms
quests.correctAnswer: Why Sectors Need Small and Large Firms
quests.hint: Ask what each kind of organization does that the other cannot, then decide what that pattern adds up to.
quests.explanation: The quick trials and the consultations are contrasts within the argument. Small organizations innovating faster is only half the pattern; the passage says each type does what the other cannot.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the division of labor in which each type does what the other cannot.
